strengths: The paper introduces a novel, well-motivated notion of group fairness for optimal transport (matching probability quotas between sensitive subgroups), clearly distinguished from prior individual-fairness and participation-based notions in matching, and from prior OT-fairness work that uses OT as an auxiliary tool for downstream prediction tasks.

Solid theoretical development: the FairSinkhorn algorithm is derived cleanly from the Lagrangian of the constrained entropic OT problem (Proposition 3.3), mirroring the classical Sinkhorn structure with an added projection step, and existence/uniqueness of the exact fair transport plan is established (Proposition 3.2) with a full proof in the appendix.

Two complementary and well-motivated relaxation strategies (convex penalization and bilevel cost learning) are proposed, with a clear and useful discussion of their tradeoffs (convexity vs. flexibility/interpretability/reusability), addressing the practically important 'price of fairness' problem.

Non-trivial statistical guarantees are provided for both relaxations: a sample-complexity bound for penalized entropic OT that matches standard (non-penalized) entropic OT rates, and a novel finite-sample deviation bound for the fairness of transport plans induced by a learned cost on unseen data. Proof sketches are given in the main text and detailed proofs (extending Rigollet & Stromme's techniques) are provided in the appendix.

Experiments, though synthetic, illustrate the intended qualitative behavior clearly: FairSinkhorn achieves perfect fairness at high cost, standard Sinkhorn is efficient but unfair, and penalized OT/cost learning interpolate between them; the reusability experiment convincingly shows a 3-4 order of magnitude inference-time advantage for the learned-cost approach over re-solving penalized OT on new batches.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on small-scale synthetic data (2D Gaussian mixtures and concentric circles with tens to a few thousand points); no real-world dataset (e.g., school admissions, kidney exchange, or dating platform data) is used despite these being the primary motivating applications throughout the introduction, which limits the demonstrated practical significance of the method.

There is no empirical comparison against any existing fairness-in-matching baseline (e.g., the participation-constrained kidney-exchange formulations or the average-utility-based fairness of Lobo et al., which the authors identify as closest prior work); the empirical evaluation only compares the paper's own three proposed variants against each other and against vanilla Sinkhorn.

The deviation bound in Theorem 4.4 has an exponential dependence on 1/ε, and while the authors note this is a known worst-case phenomenon in the entropic OT literature, no empirical assessment is given of how tight or vacuous this bound is in the experimental regimes used (e.g., ε=2), leaving the practical usefulness of the bound unclear.

The bilevel cost-learning problem is non-convex and solved via iterative differentiation with no convergence or optimization-quality guarantees; the paper's theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.4) implicitly presumes access to the (near-)optimal θ, but nothing is said about whether the gradient-based bilevel procedure used in practice reliably finds such solutions.

Presentation has clear rough edges: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated with near-identical headings and text ('Approaches and Metrics'), and the appendix contains unresolved citation placeholders ('? ]'), suggesting insufficient proofreading before submission.

Sample-complexity results are stated only for the balanced case n=m 'for simplicity,' and the extension to generic convex penalties (with an extra log(n) factor) is only asserted, not proven, limiting the generality actually established in the paper.

There is no discussion of how a central planner would realistically specify the fairness target matrix F in practice, nor any sensitivity analysis to misspecified fairness targets, nor any discussion of potential unintended consequences of enforcing rigid group-level matching quotas (e.g., interactions with individual welfare or incentive effects), despite the paper's motivating discussion of high-stakes applications like school admissions and kidney exchange.

strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated, and flexible notion of group fairness for optimal transport (target matching probabilities between sensitive-attribute groups) that generalizes and differs meaningfully from prior individual-fairness and participation-based fairness notions in matching (Gale-Shapley variants, kidney exchange literature) as well as from prior fairness-OT connections that use OT as a tool for downstream fair prediction.

Provides a complete algorithmic and theoretical package: (1) FairSinkhorn for exact fairness via a dual/Bregman-projection argument with a convergence guarantee, (2) a convex penalized relaxation solvable via generalized conditional gradient, and (3) a bilevel cost-learning relaxation, giving practitioners a spectrum of options with different convexity/interpretability/reusability trade-offs (nicely summarized in Sec. 4.3).

Non-trivial statistical guarantees are derived: a sample complexity bound for penalized entropic OT matching the rate of standard entropic OT (extending Genevay et al./Rigollet-Stromme machinery to the penalized setting, and noted to generalize to arbitrary convex penalties), and a finite-sample deviation bound for the fairness of the learned-cost transport plan on unseen data, with proofs that are detailed and appear technically sound.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation on two synthetic geometries (Gaussian mixtures, concentric circles) illustrating utility-fairness trade-off curves across all proposed methods, plus a dedicated experiment quantifying the practical reusability/inference-time advantage of learned costs versus repeatedly solving penalized OT (3-4 orders of magnitude speedup).
weaknesses: All experiments are on small synthetic datasets (Gaussians, circles); despite the paper's motivating real-world examples (school admissions, dating apps, kidney exchange), there is no evaluation on real or semi-realistic data, leaving open questions about scalability (larger n, higher-dimensional features) and practical behavior in realistic settings.

The deviation bound in Theorem 4.4 scales as exp(5RΘ/ε)/√n, which blows up for small ε — precisely the regime needed for sharp, low-bias transport plans — somewhat limiting the practical strength of the 'fairness on unseen data' guarantee; this limitation is acknowledged but not extensively discussed or empirically probed (e.g., no plot of the bound's tightness vs. ε).

No generalization bound is given for the full cost-learning bilevel problem (only a deviation bound for a fixed θ); the paper explicitly defers this to future work, leaving a gap in the theoretical story for the second (arguably more practically appealing) relaxation strategy.

The bilevel cost-learning problem is non-convex and the paper does not empirically or theoretically investigate sensitivity to initialization, local minima, or optimization stability beyond reporting final trade-off curves.

No empirical comparison against existing fairness-in-matching baselines (e.g., the group-fairness notion of Lobo et al. or kidney-exchange participation constraints) to contextualize how the proposed notion/methods perform relative to prior approaches, even qualitatively.

Presentation has minor rough edges: Section 5.1/5.2 appear to be an accidental duplicate ('Approaches and Metrics' heading twice with near-identical text), some citation placeholders remain unresolved in the appendix ('?' for Sinkhorn-Knopp and Adam references), and the dense multi-panel figures (e.g., Fig. 3-7) are difficult to parse without larger reproductions or clearer legends.

The practical specification of the fairness target matrix F by a 'central planner' is assumed given throughout; the paper offers illustrative examples (Example 3.2) but does not discuss how such targets would be elicited, justified, or audited in practice, which is important for the societal claims motivating the work.
